```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

`view_3d()` opens a plot in an interactive browser widget with orbit controls,
tooltips and selection. It uses WebGL 2, the browser graphics API, and the
R packages [htmlwidgets](https://www.htmlwidgets.org/) and
[svglite](https://svglite.r-lib.org/) to display the scene and its surrounding
plot elements. This article builds a viewer and links its selections to a
filter. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

## Example

The motor-car data contain weight in thousands of pounds, fuel economy in
miles per US gallon, gross horsepower and cylinder count. Model names identify
the observations. Map them to the hover text and selection key before
creating the widget.

```{r viewer-data}
cars <- data.frame(mtcars, model = rownames(mtcars))
p <- ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp, tooltip = model, data_id = model)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 4, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  coord_3d() + labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg", z = "horsepower")
```

Drag to orbit and use the wheel or a pinch gesture to zoom. Arrow keys orbit,
and the plus and minus keys zoom. Camera code copies the current angles into
a coordinate call, and Reset restores the initial view.

```{r viewer, fig.alt="Interactive motor-car scatterplot with orbit, zoom, hover and selection controls."}
widget <- view_3d(p, width = 624, height = 432, elementId = "cars-view")
widget
```

## Picking and selection

Picking identifies the primitive under the pointer by its identifier in an
offscreen image. Hover over a point to see its model name, then click it to
select that key. Shift-click or control-click adds and removes keys; clicking
empty space clears the selection. Unselected geometry dims while a selection
exists.

Rows sharing a key highlight together across layers. In the absence of a
key mapping, each row in each layer receives its own key. The default tooltip
lists mapped values. Use `tooltip = FALSE` to disable those default tooltips;
an explicit tooltip mapping still supplies its text.

```{r single-selection, fig.alt="Motor-car viewer allowing one selected model at a time."}
view_3d(p, selection = "single", width = 624, height = 432)
```

Set the selection mode to `"none"` to disable it. In a Shiny application,
the widget identifier above gives the selected keys in
`input[["cars-view_selected"]]` and camera updates in
`input[["cars-view_camera"]]`. Browser integrations can listen on the widget
element for `ggplot3d:hover`, `ggplot3d:select` and `ggplot3d:camera` events.

## Shiny applications

[Shiny](https://shiny.posit.co/) connects user inputs to reactive R expressions.
Use `view3dOutput()` for the output container and `renderView3d()` to return a
viewer whenever its inputs change. This module filters the cars by horsepower.
Its selected keys and camera values appear below the viewer. Each module's
`NS()` namespace gives its viewer and input events independent identifiers.

```{r shiny-example, eval=FALSE}
carUI <- function(id) {
  ns <- shiny::NS(id)
  shiny::tagList(
    shiny::sliderInput(ns("hp"), "Minimum horsepower", 50, 300, 50),
    view3dOutput(ns("scene"), height = "400px"),
    shiny::verbatimTextOutput(ns("events")))
}
carServer <- function(id) {
  shiny::moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    output$scene <- renderView3d({
      filtered <- cars[cars$hp >= input$hp, ]
      plot <- ggplot(filtered, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp,
        tooltip = model, data_id = model)) + geom_point_3d(size = 4) + coord_3d()
      view_3d(plot)
    })
    output$events <- shiny::renderPrint(list(
      selected = input$scene_selected, camera = input$scene_camera))
  })
}
ui <- shiny::fluidPage(carUI("first"), carUI("second"))
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  carServer("first")
  carServer("second")
}
shiny::shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Inside the module, use the local input names `scene_selected` and
`scene_camera`. The browser sends events with the output container's
namespaced identifier. Leave `elementId` unset in `view_3d()` so Shiny
assigns that identifier.

## Several panels

Facets stay interactive and retain their strips, titles and legends. The
example splits the cars by transmission, with zero denoting automatic and
one manual. Orbiting either panel turns both by the same amount, retaining
their relative camera angles.

```{r multi-panel, fig.height=6, fig.alt="Two vertically stacked live panels for automatic and manual cars with linked cameras."}
panels <- p + facet_wrap(~am, ncol = 1,
  labeller = as_labeller(c("0" = "automatic", "1" = "manual")))
view_3d(panels, width = 624, height = 576, link = TRUE)
```

Set `link = FALSE` to move the panel under the pointer alone. An index in
`panel` selects one facet without the surrounding plot elements. The viewers
below show automatic and manual cars separately. A shared string links
their camera changes on the same page.

```{r separate-panels, fig.alt="Automatic cars in a selected facet linked by camera group to the manual-car view below."}
view_3d(panels, panel = 1, link = "cars-cameras", width = 624, height = 432)
```

The second viewer uses the same link name. Orbit, zoom and reset changes
travel between the two, with angle changes added and zoom factors multiplied.

```{r linked-panel, fig.alt="Manual cars in a selected facet sharing camera changes with the automatic-car viewer above."}
other <- panels + coord_3d(azimuth = 30)
view_3d(other, panel = 2, link = "cars-cameras", width = 624, height = 432)
```

## Linking data with crosstalk

[crosstalk](https://rstudio.github.io/crosstalk/) links selections and filters
between widgets using shared row keys. Construct the plot from the shared
object's original data and pass that same shared object to the viewer.
The cylinder filter below hides cars excluded by the chosen cylinder counts.

```{r shared-data}
shared <- crosstalk::SharedData$new(cars, key = ~model, group = "cars")
linked <- ggplot(shared$origData(), aes(wt, mpg, z = hp, tooltip = model)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 4, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

The original rows let the viewer take its keys from the shared object.
Other crosstalk widgets in the group receive its selections and can send
selections back. Keep the plotted rows aligned with the shared data by
constructing the plot from that original table.

```{r crosstalk, fig.alt="Cylinder-count filter followed by the linked motor-car viewer."}
htmltools::tagList(
  crosstalk::filter_checkbox("cylinders", "Cylinders", shared, ~cyl),
  view_3d(linked, data = shared, width = 624, height = 432))
```

## Saving the widget

Save the widget as HTML to share an interactive view. This example writes
the supporting files beside the HTML; distribute the HTML and its companion
directory together. Use `selfcontained = TRUE` for a single HTML file when
Pandoc is available.

```{r save-widget}
directory <- tempfile("cars-viewer-")
dir.create(directory)
html <- file.path(directory, "cars.html")
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(widget, html, selfcontained = FALSE)
file.info(html)$size > 0
```

## Rendering behaviour

Opaque geometry uses a depth buffer. Transparent geometry uses weighted
blended order-independent transparency: linear-light colour weights and
fragment transmittances accumulate in separate passes, then composite over
the opaque scene. This approximates the colour of intersecting sheets and
keeps it independent of primitive order. Transparent scenes require the
WebGL 2 `EXT_color_buffer_float` extension. Circular markers use one GPU
instance per point and a disc fragment shader for their fill and border.
Text is drawn as plain browser text over the scene; a label is
hidden only when its anchor is clipped. Geometry, mapped colours and lighting are
transferred once; camera interaction runs in the browser.

Stereo plots use their central camera in the viewer. Static eye pairs and
anaglyphs are covered in [Camera and framing](camera.html). Use
[Documents](documents.html) to switch between an HTML viewer and a static
figure from the same knitr or Quarto chunk.
